paragraphs: All at once she snatched up his hand and, on impulse, kissed it three times.
“Oh, Lise, how wonderful!” cried Alyosha happily. “You know, I was absolutely sure you meant it.”
“Sure? Honestly!” She pushed his hand away but didn’t let go of it, blushing hotly and laughing a happy little laugh. “I kiss his hand and he says, ‘How wonderful!’”
But the reproach was unfair. Alyosha, too, was thoroughly flustered.
“I’d like to please you always, Lise, but I don’t know how,” he mumbled, blushing as well.

“Alyosha, dear, you’re cold and rude. Do you see? He’s picked me for his wife and he’s perfectly settled about it. He was sure I meant it. What a thing to say! Why, that’s impertinence—that’s what it is.”
“Why, was it wrong of me to be sure?” Alyosha asked, laughing suddenly.
“Oh, Alyosha, no, on the contrary, it was wonderfully right,” cried Lise, looking at him tenderly and happily.
Alyosha stood there, still holding her hand in his. Suddenly he bent down and kissed her on the lips.
“Oh, what are you doing?” cried Lise. Alyosha was dreadfully embarrassed.
“Oh, forgive me if I shouldn’t have.... Maybe I’m terribly stupid.... You said I was cold, so I kissed you.... But I see it was stupid.”
Lise laughed and hid her face in her hands. “And in this dress!” she burst out in the middle of her laughter. But all at once she stopped laughing and turned serious, almost stern.

“Alyosha, we’ll have to put off kissing. We’re not ready for that yet, and we’ll have a long time to wait,” she ended abruptly. “Tell me instead why you, who are so clever, so intellectual, so observant, pick a silly little girl, an invalid like me? Oh, Alyosha, I’m awfully happy, because I don’t deserve you one bit.”

“You do, Lise. In a few days I’ll be leaving the monastery for good. If I go out into the world, I have to marry. I know that. _He_ told me to marry, too. Who could I marry better than you—and who would have me except you? I’ve been thinking it over. First of all, you’ve known me since we were children, and you have a great many qualities I don’t have. You’re more light-hearted than I am; above all, you’re more innocent than I am. I’ve already come into contact with many, many things.... Ah, you don’t know it, but I, too, am a Karamazov. What does it matter if you laugh and make jokes, and at me, too? Go on laughing. I’m so glad you do. You laugh like a little child, but you think like a martyr.”
“Like a martyr? How?”

“Yes, Lise, your question just now, whether we weren’t showing contempt for that poor man by dissecting his soul—that was the question of someone who suffers.... You see, I don’t know how to put it, but anyone who thinks about such questions is capable of suffering. Sitting in your invalid chair, you must have thought over many things already.”

“Alyosha, give me your hand. Why are you taking it away?” murmured Lise in a faint voice, weak with happiness. “Listen, Alyosha. What will you wear when you leave the monastery? What sort of suit? Don’t laugh, don’t be angry, it’s very, very important to me.”
“I haven’t thought about the suit, Lise; but I’ll wear whatever you like.”
“I’d like you to have a dark blue velvet coat, a white piqué waistcoat, and a soft gray felt hat.... Tell me, did you believe I didn’t care for you when I said I hadn’t meant what I wrote?”
“No, I didn’t believe it.”
“Oh, you impossible person, you’re hopeless.”
“You see, I knew that you—seemed to care for me, but I pretended to believe you didn’t, to make it—easier for you.”

“That’s worse! Worse and better than anything! Alyosha, I’m awfully fond of you. Just before you came this morning, I tried my luck. I decided I’d ask you for my letter, and if you took it out calmly and handed it to me (as you might have been expected to), that would mean you didn’t love me at all, that you felt nothing and were just a stupid boy, good for nothing, and that I was ruined. But you left the letter at home, and that cheered me up. You left it behind on purpose, so as not to give it back, because you knew I’d ask for it? That was it, wasn’t it?”
“Oh, Lise, it wasn’t like that at all. The letter is with me now, and it was this morning, in this pocket. Here it is.”
Alyosha pulled out the letter, laughing, and showed it to her from a distance.
“But I’m not going to give it to you. Look at it from there.”
“Why, so you told a lie? You, a monk, told a lie!”

“I told a lie, if you like,” Alyosha laughed, too. “I told it so as not to give you back the letter. It’s very precious to me,” he added suddenly, with strong feeling, and again he flushed. “It always will be, and I won’t give it up to anyone!”
Lise looked at him joyfully. “Alyosha,” she murmured again, “look at the door. Isn’t mamma listening?”
“All right, Lise, I’ll look; but wouldn’t it be better not to? Why suspect your mother of something so mean?”

“What mean thing? As for her spying on her daughter, that’s her right, it’s not mean!” cried Lise, flaring up. “You can be sure, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that when I’m a mother, if I have a daughter like me, I’ll certainly spy on her!”
“Really, Lise? That’s not right.”

“Oh, my goodness! What does meanness have to do with it? If she were listening to some ordinary social chitchat, it would be mean, but when her own daughter is shut up with a young man.... Listen, Alyosha, do you know, I’ll spy on you as soon as we’re married, and I’ll tell you something else: I’ll open all your letters and read them, so you may as well be ready.”
“Yes, of course, if so—” muttered Alyosha, “only it’s not right.”

“Ah, how contemptuous! Alyosha, dear, let’s not quarrel on the very first day. I’d better tell you the whole truth. Of course it’s very wrong to spy on people, and of course I’m not right and you are, only I’ll spy on you all the same.”
“Go ahead, then; you won’t find out anything,” laughed Alyosha.
“And, Alyosha, will you give in to me? We have to decide that too.”
“I’d be delighted to, Lise, and I certainly will, only not in the most important things. Even if you don’t agree with me, I’ll do my duty in the most important things.”

“That’s right; but let me tell you, I’m ready to give in to you not only in the most important matters but in everything. And I’m ready to swear it now—in everything, and for all my life!” cried Lise fervently, “and I’ll do it gladly, gladly! What’s more, I’ll swear never to spy on you, not once, never to read a single one of your letters. For you’re right and I’m not. And though I’ll be awfully tempted to spy, I know I won’t do it, since you think it’s dishonorable. You’re my conscience now.... Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, why have you been so sad lately—both yesterday and today? I know you have plenty of worry and trouble, but I can see you have some special grief besides, a secret one, perhaps?”
“Yes, Lise, I have a secret one, too,” answered Alyosha mournfully. “I see you love me, since you guessed that.”
“What grief? What about? Can you tell me?” asked Lise with timid pleading.
“I’ll tell you later, Lise—afterwards,” said Alyosha, confused. “Now you might not understand it—and maybe I couldn’t explain it.”
“I know your brothers and your father are worrying you, too.”
“Yes, my brothers too,” murmured Alyosha, lost in thought.
“I don’t like your brother Ivan, Alyosha,” said Lise suddenly.
He noted this remark with some surprise, but did not answer it.

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he went on, “and my father, too. And they’re dragging others down with them. It’s ‘the primitive force of the Karamazovs,’ as Father Païssy said the other day, a crude, unbridled, earthly force. Does the spirit of God move above that force? Even that I don’t know. I only know that I, too, am a Karamazov.... Me a monk, a monk! Am I a monk, Lise? You said just now that I was.”
“Yes, I did.”
“And perhaps I don’t even believe in God.”

“You don’t believe? What’s the matter?” said Lise quietly and gently. But Alyosha did not answer. There was something too mysterious, too inward, in these last words of his, perhaps unclear even to himself, yet tormenting him.

“And now on top of it all, my friend, the best man in the world, is going, is leaving the earth! If you knew, Lise, how bound up in soul I am with him! And then I’ll be left alone.... I’ll come to you, Lise.... From now on we’ll be together.”
“Yes, together, together! From now on we’ll always be together, all our lives! Listen, kiss me, I allow you.”
Alyosha kissed her.

“Come, now go. Christ be with you!” and she made the sign of the cross over him. “Hurry back to _him_ while he’s alive. I see I’ve kept you cruelly. I’ll pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we’ll be happy! Will we be happy, will we?”
“I believe we will, Lise.”

Alyosha thought it better not to go in to Madame Hohlakov and was leaving the house without saying good-by to her. But as soon as he opened the door, he found Madame Hohlakov standing in front of him. From her very first word Alyosha guessed that she had been waiting there on purpose to meet him.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, this is awful. It’s all childish nonsense and ridiculous. I trust you won’t dream—It’s foolishness, nothing but foolishness!” she said, attacking him at once.
“Only don’t tell her that,” said Alyosha, “or she’ll be upset, and that’s bad for her now.”
“Sensible advice from a sensible young man. Am I to understand that you only agreed with her out of pity for her state as an invalid, because you didn’t want to irritate her by contradicting her?”
“Oh, no, not at all. I was quite serious in what I said,” Alyosha declared stoutly.
“To be serious about it is impossible, unthinkable, and first of all I will never be at home to you again, and I shall take her away, you may be sure of that.”
“But why?” asked Alyosha. “It’s all so far off. We may have to wait another year and a half.”

“Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that’s true, of course, and you’ll have time to quarrel and part a thousand times in a year and a half. But I am so unhappy! Though it’s such nonsense, it’s a great blow to me. I feel like Famusov in the last scene of _Sorrow from Wit_. You are Tchatsky and she is Sofya, and, just imagine, I’ve run down to meet you on the stairs, and in the play the fatal scene takes place on the staircase. I heard it all; I almost dropped. So this is the explanation of her dreadful night and her hysterics lately! It means love for the daughter but death for the mother. I might as well be in my grave at once. And a more serious matter still, what is this letter she has written? Show it to me at once, at once!”
“No, there’s no need. Tell me, how is Katerina Ivanovna now? I must know.”

“She’s still lying in delirium; she hasn’t regained consciousness. Her aunts are here, but they do nothing except sigh and put on airs. Herzenstube came, and he was so alarmed that I didn’t know what to do for him. I almost sent for a doctor to look after him. He was driven home in my carriage. And on top of it all, you and this letter! It’s true nothing can happen for a year and a half. In the name of all that’s holy, in the name of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I’m her mother. Hold it in your hand, if you like, and I’ll read it that way.”
“No, I won’t show it to you. Even if she gave her permission, I wouldn’t. I’m coming tomorrow, and if you like, we can talk over many things, but now good-by!”
And Alyosha ran downstairs and out into the street.
